Do squats and deadlifts perfectly replicate sprinting, jumping, or sport? No, but they don’t need to

Strength training develops:

✅ Maximal force
✅ Muscle mass
✅ Rate of force development
✅ Tendon/connective-tissue capacity
✅ The ability to put more force into the ground

You then practice your sport to develop the specific skill

And yes, gym strength can transfer. A meta-analysis in youth athletes found resistance training improved strength, jumping, sprinting, agility, and sport-specific performance (PMID: 26851290). A newer meta-analysis found squat training improved jump and sprint performance in team-sport athletes (PMID: 40493599)

Deadlifts aren’t merely “contextually” useful either. In a randomized trial, 10 weeks of deadlift training improved rapid torque production and vertical-jump performance (PMID: 25226322)

Does every athlete HAVE to back squat or deadlift? Of course not. Exercises are tools, not religions. Variations can be chosen based on anatomy, injury history, goals, preference, and fatigue cost. But claiming these movements inherently “compound imbalance” requires evidence. Naudi provides NONE.

Strength training is associated with LOWER sports-injury risk. One meta-analysis found strength-training interventions reduced injuries to less than one-third of control-group rates (PMID: 24100287 & 30131332). Naudi’s cable pirouettes have ZERO comparable evidence for performance or injury reduction.

Specificity matters, but he fundamentally misunderstands it. You don’t improve sprinting by only doing exercises that visually resemble sprinting. You build force and power in the gym, then sprint to apply those qualities efficiently.

I went to graduate school to uncover the dark secrets of nutrition

What I found was devastating:
Don’t chronically eat more calories than you expend
Maintain a healthy body weight

You know, the boring sh*t that works

Are individual studies sometimes flawed? Absolutely. Are there biased researchers, conflicts of interest, sloppy methods, & even misconduct? Of course. Science isn’t perfect, & it doesn’t always correct itself quickly. But it also doesn’t ask you to blindly trust one scientist or one study. Claims are supposed to survive replication, criticism, & comparison with the totality of the evidence. That matters because initial findings often get smaller, or disappear, when other researchers try to reproduce them

Compare that with social media, where someone can scream about an ingredient in a grocery-store aisle, cite a rodent study using an absurd dose, & rack up millions of views before anyone reads past the headline. People will criticize the weaknesses of research, then completely abandon that skepticism when a study supports what they already believe

Take the carnivore crowd. Many claim epidemiology is “worthless” when observational research doesn’t support their bias. But remember the famous “carnivore study”? It was an online survey of 2,029 self-selected carnivore-diet followers reporting their own health experiences. That can generate hypotheses, but it cannot show that the diet caused those outcomes or establish long-term safety. And it is about as weak as observational evidence gets. People also don’t need a check from “Big Food” to distort evidence. Personal identity, ideology, confirmation bias, & the need to defend a belief are often more than enough

The truth about nutrition is usually boring. Unfortunately, “control calories, lift weights, & eat protein & fiber” doesn’t perform as well as screaming in a grocery-store aisle: “THIS INGREDIENT IS DESTROYING YOUR HORMONES”

caption:
Your muscles literally talk to your fat.
And not in the influencer “your body is sending you messages” kind of way 😂
Skeletal muscle isn’t merely tissue that produces force, it also functions as a secretory endocrine organ. When you train, muscle releases myokines and other signaling molecules that can communicate with adipose tissue and influence its metabolism.

In 2007, Dr. @mikeormsbee  and colleagues published what was, to their knowledge, the first study to directly examine how resistance exercise affected fat metabolism within human adipose tissue. They found that lifting increased abdominal fat-cell lipolysis, the mobilization of stored fat, during and immediately after training, while also increasing post-workout fat oxidation.

More recently, researchers provided direct evidence of this “muscle-to-fat” communication in humans: after resistance exercise, muscle-specific microRNA-1 appeared to be transported to adipose tissue inside extracellular vesicles, where it influenced pathways involved in lipolysis. Now, this does not mean lifting magically deletes fat cells or overrides energy balance. You still need an energy deficit to produce meaningful fat loss.

But it does demonstrate that resistance training affects far more than the calories burned during the workout. Your muscle is metabolically active tissue that communicates with and can alter the behavior of other tissues throughout your body.

Your muscle talks to your fat. And apparently it has some pretty strong opinions. 💪

The broad consensus among sleep scientists, the American Academy of Sleep Medicine, the Society for Research on Biological Rhythms, and many other sleep researchers is that permanent Standard Time is the healthiest option—not Daylight Saving Time (DST).

The reason is that our internal circadian clock is primarily synchronized by the Sun, not by the clock on the wall. Standard Time keeps noon and sunrise closer to the Sun’s actual position, making it easier for the body’s biological clock to stay aligned.

Daylight Saving Time shifts the clock one hour later, which means darker mornings and brighter evenings. There is NO ‘best’ rep range for building muscle

The idea that you must do 8-12 reps for muscle growth because that is the ‘hypertrophy rep range’ is NOT supported by research data

Current research consistently shows that muscle growth is similar across a very wide range of rep ranges (roughly 3-30 reps), provided that:
 ✅ Sets are taken sufficiently close to failure
 ✅ Training volume is similar
 ✅ Technique is solid

That doesn’t mean all rep ranges are interchangeable.

Heavy, lower-rep training is generally more time-efficient and better for building maximal strength, but it places higher mechanical loads on joints and connective tissue (PMIDs: 33312275 & 28834797).

Higher-rep training reduces the load you have to lift, but it often creates more local fatigue and discomfort before the target muscle is fully challenged (PMID; 32401690).

The “best” rep range isn’t a magic number, it’s the one that lets you train hard, recover well, stay consistent, and progressively overload over months and years. It’s also a rep range that you enjoy doing and will be consistent with

Stop chasing the perfect rep range. Start chasing progressive overload and consistency.

firstComment:
The broad consensus among sleep scientists, the American Academy of Sleep Medicine, the Society for Research on Biological Rhythms, and many other sleep researchers is that permanent Standard Time is the healthiest option—not Daylight Saving Time (DST).

The reason is that our internal circadian clock is primarily synchronized by the Sun, not by the clock on the wall. Standard Time keeps noon and sunrise closer to the Sun’s actual position, making it easier for the body’s biological clock to stay aligned.

Daylight Saving Time shifts the clock one hour later, which means darker mornings and brighter evenings. Those brighter evenings delay the release of melatonin, making it harder for many people to fall asleep. Darker mornings also make it harder to wake up because morning light is the strongest cue that resets the circadian clock.

This is one reason researchers see increases in heart attacks, strokes, traffic crashes, and workplace injuries in the days immediately after the spring transition to DST. Even after people adjust to the one-hour shift, many sleep scientists argue that permanent DST would leave much of the population chronically out of sync with solar time, especially during winter.

So if the choices are:

* Changing clocks twice a year: not ideal.
* Permanent Daylight Saving Time: better than switching twice yearly for some practical reasons, but not the healthiest.
* Permanent Standard Time: the option most sleep experts recommend.

caption:
Your metabolism isn’t “broken.” It’s adaptive. 

It’s doing what it’s supposed to do to keep you alive When you diet, you’re sending your body a very clear signal: energy availability is low. So your body does what biology designed it to do: it tries to conserve (PMID: 21677272).

You weigh less, so it costs fewer calories to move around (PMID: 26399868). Your subconscious activity may drop (PMID: 15102614). Resting energy expenditure can decrease beyond what we’d predict from weight loss alone (PMID: 27136388). Hunger often goes up (PMID: 22475574). And suddenly, the calorie deficit that was producing weight loss at the start… isn’t the same deficit anymore.

That’s metabolic adaptation.

Not starvation mode.
Not metabolic damage.
Not “calories don’t matter.”

It’s your body adapting to a lower energy intake and a lower body weight. This is why fat loss isn’t linear. It’s why plateaus happen. And it’s why successful dieting requires adjustments, patience, and a plan instead of panic.

In this episode of The Dr. Layne Norton Podcast, I do a deep dive on what metabolic adaptation actually is, what people get wrong about it, and what you can do when fat loss stalls. Listen now wherever you get podcasts.

caption:
Welcome back to the Fiber Channel LOL

Yes, I love protein and protein matters, but if you’re sleeping on fiber, you’re missing one of the most consistently underrated nutrition levers for long-term health.

A new NHANES analysis (PMID: 42182946) looked at 9,322 adults with accelerated biological aging and followed mortality outcomes over time. Compared to the lowest fiber quartile, the highest fiber quartile had:

⬇️ 35% lower all-cause mortality risk
⬇️ 49% lower cardiovascular mortality risk

And this wasn’t some massive difference in intake. The comparison was roughly ~20.6 g/day or more versus ~9.6 g/day or less. That’s basically the difference between “almost no fiber” and “still probably not enough, but at least you tried.” Now, important caveat: this is observational data. It does NOT prove fiber magically makes you live longer. People who eat more fiber may also do other health-promoting things.

But this finding fits with a much larger body of evidence showing that higher fiber intake is associated with lower risk of cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes, colorectal cancer, and mortality (PMID: 40651334). Mechanistically, this also makes sense: fiber can improve LDL cholesterol, glycemic control, satiety, gut microbiome fermentation, short-chain fatty acid production, bowel regularity, and systemic inflammation.

So no, fiber isn’t sexy. But you know what else isn’t sexy? Dying early because you thought vegetables were “rabbit food.”

Eat your protein.
Lift your weights.
And get your damn fiber

Some of my musings as a fitness coach after many years in this space…

I’ve been observing the conversations happening in fitness lately, and I can’t help but notice how quickly the goalposts move. One minute we’re optimizing every bite of food and every biomarker. The next we’re romanticizing being as small as possible again. Then we’re told that if we aren’t taking the newest peptide or trying the latest supplement, we’re falling behind. One side of the internet is shaming another and fueling angry algorithms for things that should be free of that kind of discourse. The names and packaging keep changing what we are told and sold but underneath it all, it’s often the same ole’ promise: maybe this is finally the thing that will make you good/fit/happy/better enough.

What breaks my heart isn’t even that these conversations exist. It’s watching so many people become so consumed by the trends, the influencers, watching other people live their lives, and the endless stream of “better” that they miss their own lives. They live online more than in real life. They skip the outings to control food because of a fear of seed oils or gaining weight. They spend vacations worrying instead of being present and crash dieting beforehand. They postpone photos, celebrations, and memories until they feel “ready.” Somewhere along the way, the pursuit of health can become the thing keeping us from living.

After years of coaching, I’ve realized I’m far less interested in helping people keep up with the pace of the internet trends than I am in helping them build something the internet can’t take from them. Confidence, a body that feels like home to take care of instead of a project, an ability to enjoy dinner with friends without mentally negotiating every bite, a resilience to let one imperfect day be just that, a single day, a self-trust that builds over time.

Meanwhile the same person is eating out every day and doordash is their most frequently used app. This is one of those cases where you can ‘track’ but you’re probably getting it wrong. When you eat out, most people have no clue how much fat gets added during cooking, it’s CRAZY. 

I’m not saying you can never eat out, but you need to have proper tools and strategies in place to be able to manage it properly.

Whatever you think is in the food, track MORE. I typically add 30-50% to what I’d normally think is in the food. This gives me a cushion

I don’t get dessert when I eat out. The food is already a treat and calorie dense. Getting dessert will likely compound the issue. If I plan to get dessert then I order a very lean protein and veggies for dinner and ask for no oil or butter

I ‘bank’ macros throughout the day so I have more available for when I eat out

Another ‘hack’ if you don’t want a ton of extra butter or oil is to tell the you’re allergic. It’s not actually a real thing but most restaurants are cautious about liability and will likely comply.

In the words of the great @tonybaker “Maaan, shut the hell up!” 🤫

This is the classic wellness sleight of hand:

Take “you can make progress with less” and quietly turn it into “less is optimal.” 😂

Can you build muscle with 20-minute workouts? Absolutely. You can also get stronger doing one hard set per exercise. But minimum effective dose ≠ optimal dose.

Recovery matters, but recovery only allows you to adapt to the training stimulus you actually provided. You cannot aggressively recover from sets you never performed. The evidence consistently shows that higher resistance-training volumes generally produce more muscle growth, although the benefits eventually diminish:

A recent meta-regression of 67 studies by @josh.datadrivenstrength & @jake.remmert.phd found that hypertrophy increased as weekly set volume increased, with diminishing returns rather than some magical 20-minute cutoff (PMID: 41343037)

An earlier meta-analysis by @bradschoenfeldphd also found a graded dose-response relationship between weekly sets and hypertrophy (PMID: 27433992)

In resistance-trained men, higher-volume training produced greater hypertrophy than lower-volume training, even though strength gains were relatively similar (PMID: 30153194)

A network meta-analysis containing 119 hypertrophy studies ranked multiset training as the most effective prescription for muscle growth (PMID: 37414459)

Does this mean you should perform unlimited junk volume? Of course not. Fatigue rises, returns diminish, and your recoverable volume is individual. But if your goal is to build muscle, doing more productive hard sets within your ability to recover generally builds more muscle than doing fewer. So yes, recovery matters. But you can’t out-recover an underdose 😘

A steak at 7pm becomes an ER visit at 1am, and the chart says allergic reaction of unknown origin.

That is the diagnostic failure at the center of alpha gal syndrome. Symptoms hit six hours after the trigger: abdominal pain, hives, vomiting, difficulty breathing. Nobody asks what you ate that evening, so patients cycle through repeat ER visits before anyone connects the two.

Reaction risk is not constant. A sensitized patient can eat a burger one day with zero response, then eat the same meal the next day and end up in the ER. Heat illness is a spectrum. Heat cramps need rest and oral electrolytes. Heat exhaustion requires getting out of the heat, cooling down, and hydrating. Heat stroke is a medical emergency; cold-water immersion within 30 minutes saves lives. Do not wait.

For activity under one hour, water is enough. Over one hour, add an electrolyte drink with adequate sodium. Drink to thirst; overhydrating with plain water can cause dangerously low sodium. And acclimatize over 7 to 14 days. That is the single most effective prevention strategy.

caption:
Resting between sets isn’t being lazy. It’s crucial for building muscle

If you rush into your next set while you’re still excessively fatigued, you’ll typically perform fewer reps, produce less force, and accumulate less high-quality volume. In other words, shorter rest periods can make each individual set less stimulative on a per-set basis

One study compared 1-minute versus 5-minute rests and found that the early post-workout increase in myofibrillar protein synthesis was approximately 76% with short rests versus 152% with longer rests (PMID: 27126459). That doesn’t prove that protein synthesis after one workout perfectly predicts long-term growth, but it certainly doesn’t support the idea that gasping for air between sets is magically more anabolic

Longer rests also tend to let you maintain more repetitions and volume across subsequent sets. In trained lifters, 3-minute rests have even produced greater strength and quadriceps growth than 1-minute rests (PMID: 26605807). This was confirmed by a recent meta-analysis demonstrating that rest periods shorter than 60-90 seconds impaired hypertrophy vs. longer rest periods (PMID: 39205815)

This changes how we think about the “anabolic cap” for a single muscle in one workout. With longer rests and high-quality sets, diminishing returns may become substantial somewhere around 6–10 sets per muscle per session. If you insist on very short rests, you may need something closer to 10–15 sets to accumulate a similar amount of productive work.

Those are practical ranges, not magical biological cutoffs. Newer per-session volume research suggests diminishing returns become increasingly apparent at roughly 11 fractional sets per muscle, but individual responses and exercise selection matter (DOI: 10.51224/SRXIV.460)

My recommendation? Rest until you feel physically and mentally ready to give the next set 100% focus. That might mean 3–5+ minutes before another hard set of squats, but only 1–2 minutes before machine curls or lateral raises. 

Don’t start the next set because the clock told you to. Start it because you’re ready to make it count

caption:
What if gestational diabetes risk is influenced not only by body weight, but also by the metabolic quality of your muscle tissue?

Skeletal muscle is the primary site of glucose disposal after a meal. During pregnancy, insulin resistance increases as a normal physiological adaptation. When muscle tissue has reduced insulin sensitivity or increased intramuscular fat; a condition known as myosteatosis, glucose disposal may become less efficient, contributing to elevated blood sugar levels.

Research suggests that body composition provides insight beyond BMI alone. Higher skeletal muscle mass and lower levels of excess body fat are associated with improved metabolic health and may help reduce gestational diabetes risk. Regular exercise during pregnancy, including resistance training and walking, has been shown to lower the likelihood of developing gestational diabetes, while adequate protein intake helps support muscle maintenance throughout pregnancy.

The scale tells you how much you weigh. Muscle helps determine how effectively your body manages energy and glucose. Those are related, but they are not the same thing.
